title: Correlated Policy Optimization in Multi-Agent Subteams
claim: Restricting the coordination structure to sparser dependency graphs leaves a persistent suboptimality gap that shrinks as more correlation is allowed.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared y-axis, log-scale x, increasing agent count
description: Three line-plot panels titled Coordination Game with N=2, N=3 and N=5 agents. Each panel shows normalized suboptimality (y-axis) against iterations on a log-scale x-axis from 10^0 to about 3x10^4. Curves are colored by DAG topology, each with a shaded standard-error band. The N=2 panel compares full (black) and product (purple). The N=3 panel adds line (red) and 1+2 (blue). The N=5 panel has full, line, 1+4 (cyan), 2+3 (blue) and product. All curves start near 0.5-0.6 and drop sigmoidally around 10^2 iterations. The full-correlation policy converges to near zero. Sparser topologies plateau at higher values, with product highest at roughly 0.07-0.15. Legends sit in the upper right of each panel, and the eye goes to the plateau gaps on the right.
caption: Results of tabular softmax BN policy gradient ascent under various DAG topologies. Averaged over 50 seeds, with shaded areas showing standard error; normalized suboptimality at iteration t is defined as 1 −Vθt(µ)/V∗(µ) and initial policy θ0 ∼N(0, 1).
abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents often face scalability challenges due to the exponential growth of the joint action and observation spaces. Inspired by the structure of human teams, we explore subteam-based coordination, where agents are partitioned into fully correlated subgroups with limited inter-group interaction. We formalize this structure using Bayesian networks and propose a class of correlated joint policies induced by directed acyclic graphs . Theoretically, we prove that regularized policy gradient ascent converges to near-optimal policies under a decomposability condition of the environment. Empirically, we introduce a heuristic for dynamically constructing context-aware subteams with limited dependency budgets, and demonstrate that our method outperforms standard baselines across multiple benchmark environments.
